analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for consumers to erase credit card and other debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 315-113 on March 19, 2003, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites federal bankruptcy law around a "means test": if your income is above your state's median, the law presumes you are abusing bankruptcy, and you can be forced out of a Chapter 7 debt wipe-out and into a 3-to-5-year repayment plan instead. It also adds paperwork hurdles (mandatory credit counseling before filing, a financial management course before discharge, attorney liability for filings that later fail), extends the waiting period between Chapter 7 filings from 6 to 8 years, and caps the homestead exemption at $125,000. Scattered through it are real protections: child support moves to first priority, retirement savings and education savings accounts are shielded from creditors, family farmer bankruptcy protection becomes permanent, and a title added on the House floor raises what workers and retirees of bankrupt companies can recover. The core effect, though, is that more debtors repay more money to credit card banks and other lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card banks and other unsecured lenders, who recoup more from debtors who would otherwise discharge their debts; credit counseling agencies, which gain a mandatory pre-filing customer base; landlords, who can proceed with some evictions despite bankruptcy; and, in narrower provisions, family farmers and fishermen, child-support recipients, workers and retirees of bankrupt companies, and consumers who get new credit card disclosures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card banks and other lenders

how_it_helps.text: It flips the presumption in bankruptcy: debtors whose income exceeds their state median are presumed to be abusing Chapter 7 and can be dismissed or converted into repayment plans unless they document special circumstances.

It requires every consumer debtor to complete credit counseling before filing and a financial management course before discharge, and it extends the gap between Chapter 7 discharges from six to eight years.
It caps the homestead exemption at $125,000 for property bought within roughly the preceding three years and makes luxury purchases and recent cash advances nondischargeable.
It moves domestic support obligations (alimony and child support) into first priority, makes them harder to discharge, and lets collection proceedings proceed despite the bankruptcy stay.

It protects retirement funds and education savings accounts from the bankruptcy estate, and it makes family farmer Chapter 12 relief permanent, raises the qualifying debt limit to $3.237 million, and extends coverage to family fishermen.

A title added at the House report stage raises the priority wage and benefit ceiling for workers of bankrupt companies from $4,000 to $10,000, extends the fraudulent-transfer look-back to two years, and lets courts reinstate retiree benefits cut in the 180 days before filing.
It requires credit card companies to add minimum-payment warnings and a toll-free number so borrowers can learn how long repayment would take.

analysis.who_pays: People filing bankruptcy, especially households above their state median income who would be pushed into multi-year repayment plans; debtors who bear the cost and delay of mandatory counseling and courses; and bankruptcy attorneys, who face court-ordered fee liability for filings that courts later find abusive, a cost that typically flows back to clients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debtors above median income and their lawyers

drawbacks.text: The means test uses rigid IRS expense allowances and lets the presumption of abuse be rebutted only with documented special circumstances, which consumer advocates said would force working families facing job loss, medical bills, or divorce into repayment plans they cannot sustain.

The mandatory pre-filing counseling requirement adds a cost and waiting step for every debtor, and the bill restricts who can advise debtors and penalizes attorneys for filings that fail, raising the price of legal help at the moment people can least afford it.

The bill lengthens the wait between Chapter 7 discharges to eight years and blocks Chapter 13 discharges within four years of a prior filing, limiting the "fresh start" for people hit by repeated hard luck.

Supporters argued in good faith that some debtors with real ability to repay were using Chapter 7 to walk away from debts, and that the bill targeted repeat and fraudulent filers rather than ordinary hardship cases below median income.
It caps the homestead exemption at $125,000 for recently acquired homes, narrowing a protection some states offered homeowners facing bankruptcy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles genuinely useful protections — child support priority, retirement and education savings shields, stronger recovery for workers and retirees of bankrupt companies, permanent family farmer relief, and clearer credit card disclosures. But the core of the bill is the credit industry's decade-long goal: a means test that routes debtors with any income above their state median into repayment rather than a fresh start, backed by counseling mandates and attorney liability that raise the cost of filing. The consumer protections are real but peripheral to the bill's main effect, which is to shift billions in losses from lenders to debtors.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin, the Senate received it and placed it on its calendar, but no Senator ever voted on it, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill 18-11 on March 12, 2003, and the full House passed it 315-113 on March 19, 2003, with 225 of 228 Republicans and 90 of 205 Democrats in favor.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to protect alimony and child support from competing creditor claims failed 150-276, with 149 Democrats and no Republicans in support.
The Senate received the bill on March 20, 2003, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar under General Orders, where it remained without a vote.
The 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005, and the bill was never taken up, so it never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary debtors are better off in the short run, since the means test and counseling mandates never took effect from this bill; lenders who had pushed the measure for years gained nothing from this Congress, though the House had already shown a large majority was willing to pass it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday debtors; lenders had to wait

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 225-0 among Republicans and 90-112 among Democrats; the child-support motion to recommit split 149-52 among Democrats and 0-224 among Republicans.

industries.industry: Credit card banks and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill's means test, longer discharge waiting periods, and tighter nondischargeability rules mean more debtors repay credit card debt instead of wiping it out. Lenders' recovery comes directly at debtors' expense.

The bill makes counseling mandatory before filing and a financial course mandatory before discharge, creating a captive market of every bankruptcy filer. Debtors pay for a gatekeeper the bill itself creates.

The bill exposes debtor attorneys to court-ordered fee reimbursement and penalties for filings later found abusive and tightens who may advise debtors. Those costs typically raise the price of legal help for people filing.

The bill denies the bankruptcy stay in certain eviction cases where the landlord has a prior judgment or certifies drug use or endangerment, letting landlords proceed against tenants despite bankruptcy.
The bill makes Chapter 12 farmer bankruptcy relief permanent, raises the debt ceiling to $3.237 million, and extends coverage to fishermen, letting farm families reorganize rather than liquidate.

Title XV cracks down on corporate bankruptcy abuse: it extends the fraudulent-transfer look-back to two years, raises worker wage priority to $10,000 over 180 days, and lets courts reinstate retiree benefits cut just before filing. But other provisions help well-positioned insiders, such as allowing pre-bankruptcy investment bankers to keep advising the debtor in bankruptcy.
